editorial.headline: Retailing the Materials That Make a Building
editorial.standfirst: A broad construction-material retail activity, nationally open to full foreign ownership but blocked from PMA registration across Bali.
editorial.body:
A foreign-owned company cannot register this activity in Bali today. Nationally, the position is markedly different: the activity is open to PMA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. That contrast matters because the classification is not a narrow retail niche; it covers the sale of construction materials across the practical vocabulary of building, repair and fit-out.

Its scope reaches from metal supplies—wire rope, insect screen, nails, bolts, hinges, locks, water tanks, rolling doors, awnings and sheet metal—to porcelain sanitary and wall products such as toilets, bidets, basins, baths and tiles. It also includes a substantial timber range: boards, beams, mouldings, poles, frames, doors, windows, wooden tiles and roofing, plywood, interior plywood, teak wood, particle board, chip board, veneers and plywood for concrete formwork. Clay, lime, cement and glass materials are included too, alongside roof tiles, bricks, refractory brick, floor and wall tiles, irrigation pipes, concrete rings, cement, sand, stone, plastic pipes and hoses, corrugated plastic sheet, asbestos-cement products and sanitary equipment. Direct sales are expressly outside the stated scope.

The registration pathway is available across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. Yet the Bali position is decisive for a PMA applicant. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk classification is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every part of the activity’s scope. Bali’s province-wide, permanent moratorium blocks PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. The result is a block on PMA registration in Bali, notwithstanding the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling.

This is therefore a classification where national openness should not be mistaken for local availability. The national rule permits complete foreign ownership; Bali’s operative restriction prevents the PMA registration itself. For a founder assessing this activity, the useful reading is not that the activity is partially open or commercially conditional in Bali, but that its national PMA status and Bali registration outcome point in opposite directions.
